description: Mass unemployment, the Means Test, the Jarrow Crusade and the rise of new industries.
content_html:
The Coming of Mass Unemployment

In October 1929, the Wall Street Crash in the United States triggered a global economic depression. For Britain, already struggling with high unemployment in its old staple industries, the impact was devastating. By 1932, unemployment in Britain had reached approximately 3 million — around 22 per cent of the insured workforce. In areas dependent on a single industry, the figures were far higher: in Jarrow, a shipbuilding town on the River Tyne, unemployment reached around 65 to 70 per cent after the Palmers shipyard closed in 1934.

The industries hit hardest were those concentrated in the north of England, South Wales and central Scotland — regions that had powered the Victorian economy. Coal mining, shipbuilding, steel-making, iron and textile production all saw output collapse as world trade dried up. These were not temporary difficulties but structural crises: global demand had shifted permanently away from the goods these regions produced. The human cost was enormous: families faced poverty, malnutrition, cramped housing and a profound sense of hopelessness.

Key Fact

By 1932, British unemployment stood at approximately 3 million. The worst-affected areas were northern England, South Wales and central Scotland, where staple industries — coal, shipbuilding, steel — went into severe decline. In some towns unemployment reached over 60 per cent.

The Dole and the Means Test

Unemployed workers could claim the “dole” — weekly unemployment benefit. However, the National Insurance scheme set up before the First World War had not been designed to cope with long-term mass unemployment. By 1931, the fund was effectively bankrupt. The National Government under Ramsay MacDonald introduced spending cuts to deal with the financial crisis, including a 10 per cent cut in unemployment benefit.

Most hated of all the government’s measures was the Means Test. Before a household could receive benefit, officials would visit to assess all sources of income — including any savings, lodgers’ contributions, and even the earnings of other family members. If a son or daughter was working, their wages could be counted against the family’s entitlement. Families were forced to sell furniture and possessions before qualifying for help. The Means Test was experienced as a deeply humiliating invasion of privacy and became a symbol of the state’s callousness towards the unemployed.

The Means Test hit working-class communities hard in several ways. First, it created shame: having a government official assess your home and possessions was humiliating for men raised in a culture that prized independence. Second, it created family tensions: adult children who were working might feel obliged to leave home so their wages would not reduce their parents’ benefit. Third, it was inconsistently applied: different Public Assistance Committees in different areas operated the test with varying degrees of strictness, adding to the sense of arbitrary injustice. Mass Observation surveys from the 1930s recorded widespread resentment. The Means Test remained a powerful negative memory in Labour-voting communities for decades.

Marching for Jobs — the Jarrow Crusade

The most famous act of protest against unemployment was the Jarrow Crusade of October 1936. After Palmer’s shipyard closed in 1934, Jarrow lost its economic purpose. The town’s Labour MP, Ellen Wilkinson, helped organise a march of around 200 unemployed men who walked 300 miles from Jarrow to London over 26 days to present a petition to Parliament.

The marchers were disciplined, well-organised and non-violent, deliberately distancing themselves from the communist-led Hunger Marches of the same period. They attracted public sympathy along their route, fed and sheltered by local communities. However, when the men arrived at Westminster, the government refused to receive their petition officially. Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin did not meet them. Despite its failure as a direct political action, the Jarrow Crusade became one of the most powerful symbols of the 1930s depression — a human story of dignity in the face of official indifference. Ellen Wilkinson’s book The Town That Was Murdered (1939) kept the story alive.

Key Fact

In October 1936, approximately 200 unemployed men marched 300 miles from Jarrow to London over 26 days. Led by MP Ellen Wilkinson, the march petitioned Parliament for help. The government refused to meet the marchers or act on their petition, but the crusade became an enduring symbol of 1930s suffering.

New Industries and Internal Migration

While the north suffered, a different economic story was emerging in the Midlands and the south-east of England. Light industries producing cars, radios, vacuum cleaners and processed foods were growing rapidly. Towns like Slough, Coventry, Birmingham and Dagenham saw new factories open and employment rise. The Austin, Morris and Ford car plants drew workers from as far away as South Wales and the north-east.

This uneven recovery produced significant internal migration as unemployed workers and their families moved south in search of work. The Special Areas Act of 1934 attempted to address regional inequality by designating four “special areas” — South Wales, north-east England, west Cumberland and central Scotland — for government investment. However, the initial funding was small and the impact limited. The contrast between depressed north and expanding south deepened a regional divide that would persist throughout the century.

New consumer industries preferred the Midlands and south-east for several reasons: they were closer to the largest consumer markets (London and the Home Counties), land was cheaper, road and rail links to the south were better, and there was no entrenched union culture from the old staple industries. Foreign investors — especially American companies like Ford — also preferred the south-east as a gateway to European markets. The north’s infrastructure had been built around heavy industry: railway lines ran between coalfields and ports, not between factories and consumers. Retooling entire regions took decades — something that could not be achieved in the 1930s alone.
exam_tip_html: When answering an 8-mark ‘Explain Significance’ question about the Jarrow Crusade, remember that top-band answers address significance at the time (drew national attention to unemployment, showed the contrast between official indifference and public sympathy) AND significance over time (became a lasting symbol in Labour Party memory, influenced the post-war welfare settlement, is still referenced in debates about regional inequality). Don’t just describe what the march was — explain why it mattered then and why it still matters.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Depression hit Britain’s staple industries — coal, shipbuilding, steel — hardest, pushing unemployment to approximately 3 million by 1932, with some northern and Welsh towns exceeding 60 per cent joblessness.
  • The Means Test, introduced in 1931, became the most hated welfare measure of the decade — a humiliating household inspection that reduced benefit if any family member was earning.
  • The Jarrow Crusade (October 1936) symbolised the human cost of depression and official indifference; new light industries in the Midlands and south created a divided Britain — a prosperous south and a depressed north.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Means Test introduced in 1931.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• Officials visited homes to assess all sources of household income, including earnings of other family members.
• Families might be required to sell possessions before qualifying for benefit.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Jarrow Crusade of 1936.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• Approximately 200 unemployed men marched 300 miles from Jarrow to London to petition Parliament.
• The marchers were disciplined and non-violent, deliberately distancing themselves from communist-led marches.
• MP Ellen Wilkinson helped organise and lead the march.
• The government refused to receive the petition officially, and the Prime Minister declined to meet the marchers.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of mass unemployment in Britain in the early 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. the Wall Street Crash 1929 triggering the global depression) and traces the mechanism in detail — American banking collapse reduced world trade, demand for British exports collapsed, staple industries already struggling with structural decline faced catastrophic falls in orders, triggering mass lay-offs concentrated in the north and Wales.
Secure: Names a clear cause and provides a linked explanation with some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference to economic difficulty without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the uneven economic recovery of the 1930s in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. internal migration from north to south, or deepening regional inequality) and develops a chain — new light industries grew in the Midlands/south, workers moved south for jobs, northern communities hollowed out, Special Areas Act 1934 failed to bridge the gap, creating a lasting north-south divide.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation of a consequence with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Jarrow Crusade for attitudes towards unemployment in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (drew national sympathy, highlighted human cost of depression and government indifference) AND over time (became a defining memory for the Labour movement, influenced arguments for a welfare state, referenced in later debates about regional inequality). Weighs limits — government did not act directly — against longer-term cultural significance.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions of significance with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the march without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Means Test was the most significant way in which the Depression affected ordinary British people in the 1930s.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges the Means Test's impact (humiliation, family division, poverty) alongside other significant effects (mass unemployment, regional blight, internal migration, impact on health and housing). Weighs factors with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on the Means Test and other factors. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Approximately how many people were unemployed in Britain by 1932?
Which MP helped organise and lead the Jarrow Crusade in 1936?
The _____ Test, introduced in 1931, required officials to visit homes and assess all household income before granting unemployment benefit.
The Special Areas Act of 1934 designated regions including South Wales and north-east England for additional government _____ to tackle unemployment.
Match each feature of the Depression to its description:
right: Coal, shipbuilding and steel concentrated in northern England, Wales and Scotland
Household assessment introduced in 1931 to check entitlement to benefit
200-mile march by unemployed men from Tyneside to London in 1936

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Wall Street Crash trigger the global depression affecting Britain?
Approximately what percentage of the British insured workforce was unemployed by 1932?
Which industries were hardest hit by the Depression in Britain?
flashcard_questions.a: The old staple industries of the north and Wales — especially coal mining and shipbuilding — collapsed as world trade dried up.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Means Test introduced in 1931?
flashcard_questions.a: A household income assessment determining whether a family qualified for unemployment benefit.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the Means Test hated by working-class communities?
flashcard_questions.a: It was a humiliating home inspection that could count family members' earnings against benefit entitlement.

flashcard_questions.q: The Jarrow Crusade took place in _____ 1936, when _____ men marched to London.
Who was the MP who helped organise the Jarrow Crusade?
What was the government's response when the Jarrow marchers reached London?
flashcard_questions.a: The government refused to receive their petition officially or meet the marchers.

flashcard_questions.q: Which 1934 Act tried to address regional unemployment by designating four areas for government investment?
Which regions saw new light industries grow during the 1930s while the north declined?
What were 'light industries' that expanded in the 1930s?
flashcard_questions.a: Factories making consumer goods for the mass market — the car industry at Dagenham and Coventry is the clearest example.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the Palmers shipyard in Jarrow in 1934?
flashcard_questions.a: It closed, leaving around 65-70 per cent of the town unemployed.

glossary_terms.definition: Heavy industries such as coal mining, steel-making, textiles and shipbuilding that had been the foundation of Britain's Victorian economy.
An intrusive assessment introduced in 1931 to determine whether a household's total income and assets justified continued payment of unemployment benefit.
A march of 200 unemployed men from Jarrow to London in October 1936 to petition Parliament for help and draw attention to the town's unemployment crisis.
Manufacturing industries producing consumer goods such as cars, electrical appliances and processed foods, which expanded rapidly in the 1930s, especially in the Midlands and south-east.

items.title: BBC Teach — History Class Clips
items.description: BBC Teach's curriculum history channel covers the 1930s Depression, mass unemployment and the Jarrow March with short clips designed for classroom use.

items.title: Simple History — 1930s Britain
items.description: Simple History covers the human cost of the Great Depression, dole queues, the Means Test and the regional divide between the depressed north and recovering south.

items.title: The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner (1962)
items.description: Tony Richardson's British New Wave classic explores class inequality and working-class frustration — a key text for understanding the north-south divide in mid-20th-century Britain.

items.title: Hope and Glory (1987)
items.description: John Boorman's semi-autobiographical film depicts working-class life in wartime Britain, capturing the community spirit and privation that grew out of Depression-era experience.

items.title: The Spirit of '45 (2013)
items.description: Ken Loach's documentary uses first-hand testimony to trace how the suffering of the Depression and war years directly shaped the post-war demand for a welfare state.

items.title: Britannica — Great Depression
items.description: Encyclopaedia article on the global economic crisis triggered by the Wall Street Crash, explaining how it devastated British staple industries and drove unemployment to 3 million.

items.title: Britannica — William Beveridge
items.description: Biography of the economist whose report on social security was shaped directly by his study of mass unemployment in the 1930s, leading to the post-war welfare state.

items.title: Britannica — General Strike of 1926
items.description: Covers the miners' dispute and TUC solidarity action that set the context for deteriorating industrial relations in the years before the Depression struck.

items.title: Made in Dagenham (2010)
items.description: Drama about the 1968 Ford Dagenham strike by women workers — the Dagenham plant was built in the 1930s as part of the new light-industrial south that replaced depressed northern staple industries.
